structure.rationale: The 18 concepts follow the requester's own outline (issue #146), which this pass preserves verbatim rather than re-deriving: six parts moving from the core mental model (server/session/window/pane, first session) through daily fluency (pane workflow, copy mode, long-running jobs), to ownership (config, bindings, status line), to applied developer workflows (projects, SSH, reproducible workspaces — with Elixir/Phoenix and Rust worked examples per the notes), to automation (scripting, plugins, restoration), and finally advanced/team practice (debugging, sharing sessions, and a capstone personal system). Each concept page is expected to follow the same problem -> concept -> hands-on commands -> realistic workflow -> exercise -> common-mistake shape, which is why the shared stylesheet defines .callout variants for key-idea, warning, mistake, and exercise up front. The requester's appendix material (cheat sheet, annotated tmux.conf, bootstrap scripts, migration guide, glossary) is folded into existing pages rather than spawned as separate concepts, per the notes field, to keep the 18-concept structure intact.
structure.audience: Developers who already live in a terminal (shell, editor, git) but have never used tmux, or use it shallowly and want a deliberate, reproducible setup for solo and remote/pair work.

claims.text: tmux is a terminal multiplexer: a single background server process owns any number of sessions, and lightweight clients (terminal windows) attach to a session to display and control it.

A tmux session is persistent: it survives an accidental disconnection (e.g. an ssh connection timing out) or an intentional detach (prefix + d), because the programs running inside it belong to the server process, not to the client that was viewing it.
Detaching leaves the session running in the background; reattaching with `tmux attach` restores the same panes, scrollback, and running foreground jobs exactly as they were left.

tmux was written by Nicholas Marriott and first released in November 2007 under the ISC license, as a cleaner-codebase, BSD-licensed alternative to GNU Screen; it was imported into the OpenBSD base system in 2009 (OpenBSD 4.6).

tmux's session/window/pane hierarchy and its client-server split are what most sharply distinguish it from GNU Screen: tmux had native, layout-preserving vertical and horizontal splits from its first release, while Screen only gained autosaved split layouts much later (Screen 5.0); operations like switching windows are handled server-side in tmux, so every attached client sees the same state.

A terminal emulator's built-in tabs (macOS Terminal.app, GNOME Terminal, Windows Terminal, etc.) are owned by the terminal application's own process — there is no separate server, so quitting or crashing that application ends every shell inside its tabs at once, with no detach/reattach step available.

iTerm2's tmux integration mode (`tmux -CC`) attaches to a tmux session but renders its windows and panes as native iTerm2 tabs and split panes, so the session is still owned and kept alive by the tmux server while the client gets a native window-manager feel.

snippets.code:
tmux new -s work      # start a new named session
tmux attach -t work    # reattach to it later (any client, any machine with access)
# inside tmux: prefix (Ctrl-b) then d   -> detach, leaving it running
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

pitfalls: Assuming tmux only matters over SSH: the same server-owned persistence also protects local work from a crashed or accidentally-closed terminal app, an IDE restart, or a laptop reboot.

Confusing 'close the terminal window' with 'end the session': closing the surrounding terminal app just drops a client — the tmux server and its session keep running in the background and can be reattached; typing `exit` in every pane of that session, or `tmux kill-session`, is what actually ends it.
Expecting an IDE's built-in terminal panel to behave like tmux: it is tied to the editor process's lifetime, so closing or crashing the IDE takes every job in it down with no reattach option.

claims.text: tmux is installed from the OS package manager on every mainstream platform: `sudo apt install tmux` (Debian/Ubuntu), `brew install tmux` (macOS via Homebrew), `sudo dnf install tmux` (Fedora), `sudo pacman -S tmux` (Arch); `tmux -V` prints the installed version to confirm.
`tmux new -s NAME` (short for `new-session -s NAME`) creates a new session named NAME and immediately attaches the current terminal to it as a client.
If `-s` is omitted, tmux assigns the session an automatic numeric name starting at 0 (then 1, 2, ...) instead of a memorable one, which makes it harder to target later with `attach -t`.
The default prefix key is Ctrl-b: nearly every tmux command from inside a session is invoked by pressing Ctrl-b, releasing it, then pressing a single command key (e.g. Ctrl-b then d).
Detaching (prefix d, or running `tmux detach-client`) disconnects the client from the session without ending any process inside it; the session keeps running on the server.

`tmux ls` (short for `list-sessions`) lists every session on the server with its window count, creation time, and marks the currently-attached session; `tmux attach -t NAME` (or `tmux a -t NAME`) reattaches to a specific one by name, while `tmux attach` with no `-t` attaches to the most recently used session, not a chosen one.

`tmux new -A -s NAME` is idempotent: it attaches to the session NAME if it already exists, or creates it if it doesn't, which makes it safe to bind as a single 'go to my session' command run from any shell startup or launcher. The -A flag was added in tmux 1.8 (2013).
`tmux kill-session -t NAME` ends a session outright (kills every process inside it), which is different from detaching (prefix d), which merely stops watching it.

tmux tracks whether the current shell is already inside a session via the $TMUX environment variable it sets on attach; running `tmux` again from inside an existing session tries to nest and fails with 'sessions should be nested with care, unset $TMUX to force' rather than silently creating a confusing session-inside-a-session.

The default status line sits at the bottom of the terminal: the left side shows the current session name in brackets, the middle lists the session's windows by index with the active one marked, and the right side shows the host name and clock — all customizable later, but present unmodified from the first session onward.

snippets.code:
# pick one for your platform, then confirm
sudo apt install tmux        # Debian / Ubuntu
brew install tmux            # macOS (Homebrew)
sudo dnf install tmux        # Fedora
sudo pacman -S tmux          # Arch
tmux -V                       # -> tmux 3.x

tmux new -s work        # create + attach a session named "work"
# ...work happens...
# Ctrl-b, release, then d   -> detach, session keeps running

tmux ls                  # -> work: 1 windows (created ...) (attached)
tmux attach -t work      # or: tmux a -t work

tmux kill-session -t work   # ends it outright, unlike detaching
snippets.note: the full first-session loop: create, detach, list, reattach, end

snippets.code: tmux new -A -s work   # attaches to "work" if it exists, creates it if not
snippets.note: idempotent create-or-attach, safe to run repeatedly

pitfalls: Skipping -s and getting a numeric session name (0, 1, 2, ...): it works, but weeks later `tmux ls` is the only way to remember what's what — name every session on purpose.

Running `tmux` again from inside an already-attached session tries to nest and fails with 'sessions should be nested with care, unset $TMUX to force'; detach first (prefix d) and reattach, rather than fighting the warning.
Assuming `tmux attach` with no `-t` will ask which session to open: it silently attaches to the most-recently-used one, which is the wrong session as soon as more than one exists.

Reading the status line's session name in brackets as a window title, or the window list in the middle as a list of sessions — the three zones (session / windows / host+clock) are easy to conflate on a first look.

claims.text: tmux's object model is a strict hierarchy: one server process holds any number of sessions; each session holds one or more windows; each window holds one or more panes, which are the actual shells/programs running side by side inside a window.

A window is a single full-screen layout (of one or more panes) shown at one time; a session is really just a named list of windows plus which one is currently active, and a client only ever displays one window of one session at a time.

Objects are addressed with a target string of the form session:window.pane (e.g. work:1.2 = pane 2 of window 1 in session work); if a target is left partially or fully unqualified, tmux fills in the current session/window/pane, which is convenient interactively but should be written fully qualified in scripts.

By default, window and pane indexes are zero-based (the first window is 0, the first pane in it is 0); this is a common surprise for people used to 1-based counting, and is controlled by the base-index and pane-base-index session options (set later, in configuration).

prefix c runs new-window, creating a new window in the current session and switching to it; prefix , runs command-prompt to rename the current window; prefix & runs kill-window (with a confirmation prompt) to close the current window and everything in it.

Window navigation: prefix n / prefix p move to the next/previous window; prefix 0-9 jumps directly to that window index; prefix w opens an interactive, searchable list of all windows to choose from; prefix l jumps back to the last (previously) selected window, a fast toggle between two windows.

prefix % runs split-window -h, splitting the current pane into a left and right pair (a vertical dividing line); prefix " runs split-window -v, splitting it into a top and bottom pair (a horizontal dividing line) — the -h/-v flags name the split line's orientation, not the resulting pane arrangement, which is the single most common point of confusion for new users.

Pane navigation and management: prefix + arrow key moves focus to the pane in that direction; prefix o cycles focus to the next pane; prefix q briefly overlays each pane with its number, and pressing that number jumps straight to it; prefix x runs kill-pane (with confirmation) to close just that pane, leaving the rest of the window intact; prefix z runs resize-pane -Z to toggle zooming the current pane to fill the whole window (and back).
Closing the last pane in a window closes the window; closing the last window in a session ends the session (and, if it was the last session on the server, the server itself exits).

prefix ! runs break-pane, promoting the current pane out into its own new window; prefix { and prefix } run swap-pane -U / swap-pane -D to swap the current pane's position with the previous/next pane in the window's layout order, without changing focus.

A pane's program exiting (e.g. the shell inside it exits) closes that pane automatically; tmux does not ask for confirmation in that case the way it does for prefix x, since the process simply ended on its own.

snippets.code:
# from the command line (outside tmux), fully-qualified targets:
tmux new-window -t work -n build       # add a window named "build" to session work
tmux select-window -t work:2           # jump to window index 2 in session work
tmux split-window -h -t work:1         # split window 1's active pane left/right
tmux select-pane -t work:1.2           # focus pane 2 of window 1
tmux kill-window -t work:2             # close window 2 and everything in it
tmux list-windows -t work              # show every window in session work
tmux list-panes -t work:1              # show every pane in window 1
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
prefix c        new-window              prefix &   kill-window (confirm)
prefix ,        rename-window           prefix l   last-window (toggle)
prefix n / p    next / previous window  prefix w   choose-window (list)
prefix 0-9      select window by index

prefix %        split-window -h  (left | right)
prefix "        split-window -v  (top / bottom)
prefix arrows   move focus one pane over
prefix o        cycle focus to next pane
prefix q        flash pane numbers, press one to jump
prefix x        kill-pane (confirm)      prefix z   zoom/unzoom pane
prefix !        break-pane to new window prefix {}  swap-pane prev/next
snippets.note: the default (unmodified) key table; all still Ctrl-b as the second key of prefix, then the listed key

pitfalls: Assuming % gives a horizontal (stacked) split and " gives a vertical (side-by-side) one — it's the reverse: the flag names the dividing line's orientation, not the pane layout, and this trips up almost everyone at first.
Typing 1, 2, 3... expecting to jump to the "first" window with prefix 1 and landing on the second one instead, because window/pane indexes are zero-based by default.

Confusing a new window (prefix c — a whole new full-screen layout, still the same session) with a new pane (prefix % or " — a split inside the current window) — reaching for the wrong one wastes screen space or fragments work that should have stayed in one place.
Running prefix x or prefix & out of habit and blowing past the confirmation prompt without reading it, killing a pane/window with unsaved work in it.

claims.text: resize-pane (bound by default to prefix + an arrow key held with a modifier) changes a pane's dimensions without changing the layout's shape otherwise: prefix then Ctrl-Up/Down/Left/Right grows or shrinks the current pane by one cell in that direction, and prefix then Meta(Alt)-Up/Down/Left/Right does the same in five-cell steps for a bigger adjustment.

The Ctrl-arrow and Meta-arrow resize bindings are repeatable: after pressing prefix once, tmux keeps accepting the same key (held or pressed again) for the repeat-time window (500ms by default) without requiring the prefix again, so holding Ctrl and tapping an arrow several times resizes in one fluid motion instead of one prefix per cell.

resize-pane also accepts an explicit target and amount from the command line or command prompt, e.g. `resize-pane -t work:1.2 -R 10` grows pane 2 of window 1 ten cells to the right, and `resize-pane -Z` toggles zooming the current pane to fill the whole window (the same operation bound to prefix z).

tmux ships five built-in pane layouts, cycled through with select-layout: even-horizontal (panes spread evenly left-to-right, side by side), even-vertical (panes spread evenly top-to-bottom, stacked), main-horizontal (one large pane across the top, the rest in a row underneath), main-vertical (one large pane on the left, the rest stacked in a column on the right), and tiled (panes arranged in as even a grid as the pane count allows).

prefix Space runs next-layout, cycling through the five built-in layouts in order and reflowing every pane in the current window to fit the chosen layout, which is faster than hand-resizing a layout you've fought into a wrong shape.

Each built-in layout can also be selected directly, either from the command prompt (`:select-layout tiled`) or via the default bindings prefix Alt-1 through prefix Alt-5, mapped in order to even-horizontal, even-vertical, main-horizontal, main-vertical, and tiled.

prefix Ctrl-o runs rotate-window, which rotates the panes of the current window forward through the positions of the active layout (each pane's content moves to the next slot) without changing which layout is in effect or which pane has focus's relative position.

The synchronize-panes window option, toggled with `setw synchronize-panes on` (and off again the same way), makes every keystroke typed into the active pane get sent to every other pane in that window simultaneously -- not just visible characters but backspaces and cursor movement too -- so one typed command runs identically across all of them at once.

join-pane (and its mirror move-pane) relocates an existing pane from one window into another, taking `-s` (source pane) and `-t` (target window or pane) plus an optional `-h`/`-v` to say whether it joins as a horizontal or vertical split; this differs from break-pane (already covered), which does the opposite -- pulling a pane out into a brand-new window.

Setting `set -g mouse on` in tmux.conf (or running `:set -g mouse on` for the current session) turns on mouse support: clicking a pane focuses it, clicking a window's name in the status line switches to it, dragging a pane border resizes the panes on either side of it, and the scroll wheel scrolls a pane's history -- all without leaving the keyboard-driven bindings intact.

snippets.code:
prefix Ctrl-arrow    resize-pane, 1 cell   (repeatable within repeat-time)
prefix Meta-arrow     resize-pane, 5 cells  (repeatable within repeat-time)
prefix Space          next-layout           (cycle the 5 built-in layouts)
prefix Alt-1..Alt-5   select-layout directly: even-h, even-v, main-h, main-v, tiled
prefix Ctrl-o         rotate-window         (rotate pane positions forward)
snippets.note: default bindings, verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
# resize pane 2 of window 1 in session work, 10 cells to the right, from outside
tmux resize-pane -t work:1.2 -R 10

# jump straight to a named layout instead of hand-resizing
tmux select-layout -t work:1 tiled

# move a pane living in window 2 into window 1, as a new right-hand split
tmux join-pane -h -s work:2.1 -t work:1
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
# run the same command on three hosts side by side
tmux new -s fleet
Ctrl-b %
Ctrl-b %
# ssh into three different hosts, one per pane, then:
Ctrl-b :setw synchronize-panes on
# type once -- it goes to all three panes at once
sudo apt update
# turn it back off before doing anything pane-specific
Ctrl-b :setw synchronize-panes off

pitfalls: Leaving synchronize-panes on after the job it was turned on for is done: the next command typed -- including something destructive like an rm or a service restart -- goes to every pane in the window at once, not just the one you're looking at. Turn it off the moment the parallel task is finished, and treat the status line (which tmux marks while it's active) as a thing to actually glance at.

Hand-resizing panes one Ctrl-arrow tap at a time when a built-in layout already matches the shape wanted: prefix Space (or a direct prefix Alt-N) reflows the whole window in one step and is almost always faster than nudging borders into place.

Confusing join-pane's -h/-v with split-window's: both use -h for a left/right (side-by-side) result and -v for a top/bottom (stacked) result, but because join-pane operates across windows it's easy to mistype the target and join into the wrong window's layout -- `list-windows` first if unsure.

Turning on `mouse on` and then fighting it when trying to select and copy multi-line text the OS way: with mouse mode active, tmux's own click-drag takes over pane selection and copy mode instead of the terminal's native text selection, which surprises people expecting their usual triple-click-to-select-a-line behavior (the fix -- holding a modifier key while dragging, e.g. Option/Shift depending on terminal -- is terminal-specific and worth knowing before it's needed).

claims.text: Output that scrolls off the top of a pane is not gone: each pane keeps a per-pane scrollback of past lines governed by the history-limit option, but the ordinary pane view only ever shows the current screen, so the terminal's own scrollbar (if any) and normal text selection can't reach that history.

history-limit defaults to 2000 lines per pane and can be raised (e.g. `set -g history-limit 50000`), but the change only takes effect for panes created after the option is set -- existing panes keep whatever limit was in force when they were created until they're closed and reopened; very large limits trade memory for scrollback depth.

prefix [ enters copy mode: the pane freezes (new output still arrives and is appended to the history, but the visible view stops following it), a cursor appears, and the scrollback plus the current screen become one navigable, searchable buffer. prefix PageUp is a shortcut that jumps straight into copy mode already scrolled up a page, for the common case of 'I just want to look up, right now'.

Copy mode has two selectable key tables, controlled by the mode-keys option: emacs (the default on a fresh install) and vi (`set -g mode-keys vi` -- and separately `set -g status-keys vi` for the command prompt, which is a different, often-forgotten option). Which table is active changes every navigation and selection keystroke inside copy mode; it does not change any binding outside copy mode.

In the default emacs key table: arrow keys and Ctrl-a/Ctrl-e move by character/line-start/line-end, Alt-b/Alt-f move by word, PageUp/PageDown move a full screen, Ctrl-Space begins a selection, Ctrl-w (or Alt-w) copies the selection and exits copy mode, and Ctrl-s/Ctrl-r search forward/backward.

In the vi key table: h/j/k/l move left/down/up/right, w/b move by word, g/G jump to the top/bottom of the history, Ctrl-b/Ctrl-f (or PageUp/PageDown) move a full screen and Ctrl-u/Ctrl-d move a half screen, Space (or v) begins a selection, Enter (or y) copies the selection and exits copy mode, and Ctrl-v toggles rectangle (block) selection instead of the default line-wrapping selection.

Searching inside copy mode is incremental and directional: / (search-forward, vi table) or Ctrl-s (emacs table) searches toward more recent output, ? (search-backward, vi) or Ctrl-r (emacs) searches toward older output; n repeats the last search in the same direction, N repeats it in the reverse direction.

A completed copy (via copy-selection-and-cancel, the default effect of Enter/y or Ctrl-w/Alt-w) is stored as tmux's own 'paste buffer', separate from the operating system clipboard; prefix ] pastes the most recent buffer into the active pane, prefix # lists every stored buffer (list-buffers), and prefix = opens an interactive picker (choose-buffer) to paste an older one instead of only the newest.

With `set -g mouse on`, the scroll wheel drives copy mode too: the default WheelUpPane binding checks whether the pane is already in a mode, already in the terminal's alternate screen, or mouse dragging is otherwise in effect, and only then enters copy mode automatically on scroll-up -- which is why scrolling over a full-screen program like vim, less, or htop (all of which use the alternate screen and manage their own scrolling) does not drop you into tmux copy mode, while scrolling over a plain shell prompt does.

tmux's own paste buffer is not the same thing as the operating system clipboard, so pasting into another application needs a bridge: either OSC 52 (`set -g set-clipboard on`, plus, for some terminals, a terminal-overrides tweak to pass the escape sequence through) which asks the terminal emulator itself to write to the OS clipboard and works even over SSH if the terminal supports it, or piping the copied text through an external command via copy-pipe-and-cancel bound to the copy key (e.g. `xclip -selection clipboard` or `xsel` on X11, `wl-copy` on Wayland, `pbcopy` on macOS), which requires that tool to be installed locally and does not work over a remote SSH hop unless that hop also has it.

snippets.code:
# raise scrollback before creating new panes (existing panes are unaffected)
tmux set -g history-limit 50000

# switch copy mode to vi-style navigation and selection
tmux set -g mode-keys vi
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
prefix [          copy-mode                (freeze the pane, start navigating)
prefix PageUp     copy-mode, scrolled up one page already

-- vi table (set -g mode-keys vi) --
h j k l           left / down / up / right       g / G   top / bottom of history
w / b             next / previous word           Ctrl-b/Ctrl-f  page up/down
/ / ?             search forward / backward      n / N   repeat search (same/reverse)
Space or v        begin-selection                Ctrl-v  rectangle-toggle
Enter or y        copy-selection-and-cancel       q       cancel, exit copy mode

-- emacs table (default) --
arrows            move cursor                    Ctrl-a/Ctrl-e  start/end of line
PageUp/PageDown   page up/down                   Ctrl-s/Ctrl-r  search fwd/back
Ctrl-Space        begin-selection                Ctrl-w  copy-selection-and-cancel

prefix ]          paste-buffer   (most recent buffer, into the active pane)
prefix #          list-buffers   prefix =  choose-buffer (pick an older one)
snippets.note: default bindings, verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
# bridge tmux's paste buffer to the OS clipboard over SSH, via the terminal (OSC 52)
set -g set-clipboard on

# or: pipe the selection straight to a clipboard tool when copying, vi table
bind-key -T copy-mode-vi y send-keys -X copy-pipe-and-cancel "xclip -selection clipboard"
# macOS equivalent: "pbcopy"   Wayland equivalent: "wl-copy"
snippets.note: two independent approaches to reach the OS clipboard; pick one per platform/terminal

pitfalls: Typing into a pane that looks unresponsive and not realizing it's frozen in copy mode: keystrokes are being read as copy-mode navigation/search commands, not sent to the shell, until q or Enter/Ctrl-w exits it.

Assuming a raised history-limit applies retroactively: it only takes effect for panes created after the option changes, so an already-open long-running pane keeps its old, smaller scrollback until it's closed and reopened.

Confusing tmux's internal paste buffer (prefix ]) with the operating system clipboard: a copy made in copy mode is instantly pasteable into another tmux pane, but reaching another application (a browser, a chat window) needs an explicit OSC 52 or copy-pipe bridge configured in tmux.conf -- it is not automatic on a stock install.

Expecting the mouse scroll wheel to work the same everywhere: over a plain shell it enters copy mode and scrolls history, but over a full-screen program like vim or less it passes straight through to that program's own scrolling instead, because tmux detects the alternate screen and defers to it.

Searching and getting no results because the search direction was backwards from what was expected: / (or Ctrl-s) searches toward more recent output and ? (or Ctrl-r) toward older output, relative to the cursor's current position, not the top or bottom of the buffer.

claims.text: tmux's client-server model (established in why-tmux) already solves 'keep this running after I disconnect' structurally: a job running in a pane belongs to the tmux server process, not to the client watching it, so detaching (or a dropped SSH connection) does not send it SIGHUP the way closing a plain terminal window does -- which means the old habit of backgrounding a command with `&` plus `nohup`/`disown` to protect it from a closed shell is solving a problem tmux has already removed.

monitor-activity is a per-window option, off by default, enabled with `setw -g monitor-activity on` (setw is short for set-window-option); once on, any output written to a window other than the one currently displayed marks that window in the status line.

monitor-silence takes an interval in seconds and is disabled by an interval of zero (the default); set to a nonzero value, a window is flagged once it has produced no new output for that many seconds -- a more useful signal than monitor-activity for 'the build finally stopped scrolling and is either done or stuck', versus 'the build printed a single line'.

Whether a flagged window's alert is shown only as a status-line highlight or also as an on-screen message is controlled separately by visual-activity / visual-silence / visual-bell (off by default, so a plain status-line mark only); which windows the flag applies to at all is controlled by activity-action / silence-action / bell-action, defaulting to 'other' -- act only on windows other than the one currently active, since flagging the window you're already looking at is meaningless.

Because monitor-activity and monitor-silence are window options rather than session- or server-wide ones, they can be turned on for a single long-running window (a build, a deploy, a watch process) and left off everywhere else with a plain `setw` run while attached to that window, rather than a `-g` (global) flag that would apply the setting to every window in the session.

remain-on-exit is off by default: the instant a pane's running program exits, tmux closes that pane immediately (and the window too, if it was the pane's last one), which can carry away a crash message or final line of output before anyone reads it. `set -g remain-on-exit on` keeps an exited pane open -- dead, showing its last screen and full scrollback, marked inactive -- until it is explicitly dealt with.

respawn-pane restarts a command inside an existing pane (typically one left dead by remain-on-exit) without recreating the pane or disturbing its position in the window's layout; `respawn-pane -k` forces the restart even on a pane that is not dead, killing whatever is currently running in it first. respawn-window is the same operation for every pane of a whole window.

pipe-pane connects a pane's output, from that moment forward, to an external command -- e.g. `pipe-pane -o 'cat >> ~/logs/build.log'` starts appending everything the pane subsequently prints to a file. The `-o` flag makes it a toggle: running the identical pipe-pane command again turns the pipe off. It captures only output produced after it is started, not anything already on screen or already scrolled into history.

capture-pane takes a snapshot of what a pane already holds instead of watching forward: `capture-pane -p -S - -E -` prints the pane's full retained history (bounded by history-limit) plus its current screen to stdout, where -S - means 'start at the oldest history line' and -E - means 'end at the current line'. Run without -p, the captured text goes into a tmux paste buffer instead, which save-buffer can then write out to a file.

automatic-rename (a window option, on by default in modern tmux) keeps a window's name synced to what's running in its active pane, formatted by automatic-rename-format -- but naming a window manually, whether with rename-window / prefix , or a terminal escape sequence at creation, permanently switches automatic-rename off for that one window until it is explicitly turned back on, so a deliberately-named 'deploy' window keeps that name even after the deploy command finishes and the shell prompt returns.

set-titles (off by default) additionally pushes a pane's title, formatted by set-titles-string, out to the surrounding terminal emulator's own window/tab title -- relevant for anyone reading a terminal's native tabs rather than tmux's own status line, such as iTerm2's tmux -CC integration mode already covered in why-tmux.

snippets.code:
# flag this one window when it goes quiet for 30s -- scoped to the current window, not -g
tmux setw monitor-silence 30
tmux set -g visual-activity on

# ...work elsewhere; the status line marks the window once it's silent...

tmux setw monitor-silence 0   # back off once you've reattached and dealt with it
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
tmux set -g remain-on-exit on
# process in the pane exits -> pane stays, shows "Pane is dead", keeps its scrollback
# prefix [ still works on a dead pane -- read exactly what it printed before exiting
tmux respawn-pane -k    # restart the same command in the same pane, same layout slot

snippets.code:
# log everything this pane prints from now on
tmux pipe-pane -o 'cat >> ~/logs/deploy.log'
# ...run the deploy...
tmux pipe-pane            # no argument, same command -> toggles logging back off

# grab what's already in the pane's scrollback, right now, in one shot
tmux capture-pane -p -S - -E - > ~/logs/deploy-snapshot.txt
snippets.note: pipe-pane only sees output from the moment it starts; capture-pane -S - reaches backward instead

pitfalls: Setting monitor-activity with -g instead of scoping it to one window: every window in the session lights up on any ordinary output (a new shell prompt counts), and the one build or deploy actually worth watching gets lost in the noise.

Assuming pipe-pane captures the backlog already on screen when it's started: it only pipes output printed after that moment forward. Anything already printed needs capture-pane -S -, or pipe-pane needs to have been running since before the interesting output happened.

Not turning on remain-on-exit before a job that might fail at the very last line: the pane (and the window, if it was the last pane in it) closes the instant the process exits, taking a crash message or exit status with it before anyone reads it.

Renaming a window by hand and then being surprised automatic-rename stopped tracking the running command: that's the documented behavior, not a bug -- a manual rename-window (or prefix ,) permanently disables automatic-rename for that window until it's explicitly re-enabled.

claims.text: tmux reads its configuration file once, top to bottom, as a plain list of the same commands available at the tmux command prompt (prefix :) or as `tmux <command>` from the shell -- there is nothing special about config-file syntax beyond one command per line.

Config file lookup order: an explicit `-f <path>` on the tmux command line overrides everything; otherwise tmux reads `~/.tmux.conf` if it exists; failing that (and as of tmux 3.2) it falls back to `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tmux/tmux.conf`, or `~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf` if XDG_CONFIG_HOME is unset. A system-wide `/etc/tmux.conf`, if present, is read first, before the user's own file, so user settings placed after it can override system defaults.

A config file is only read automatically when a new tmux server starts. Editing it does not affect an already-running server or session until it is explicitly re-read with the `source-file` command, e.g. `tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf`; most session/window/key-binding options apply immediately on reload, though a small number of once-only startup values do not.

A common convention is to bind the reload inside the config itself, e.g. `bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display-message "reloaded"`, so re-reading the file after an edit is prefix r instead of retyping the full command.

Options live in a few separate namespaces: server options (rare -- one setting, e.g. escape-time, that applies to the whole tmux process and every client attached to it, changed with `set-option -s`), session options (changed with `set-option`/`set`), and window options (changed with `set-window-option`/`setw`). Pane options exist too but are used far less often.

Within session or window options, an optional `-g` flag controls breadth, independently of which command (set vs setw) controls which kind of object: `-g` sets the global default that every session (or window) inherits unless it has its own local override; without `-g`, the command applies only to the current session (or, for setw, the window currently attached to) -- e.g. chapter 6's `setw monitor-silence 30` with no -g, scoped deliberately to just the one window running a build.

During initial parsing of a config file at server startup, there is not yet a 'current session' for a bare (non -g) session-option command to apply to -- some such commands can fail outright with an error like 'no current session'. This is why nearly every line in a starting tmux.conf uses `-g`; a bare `set`/`setw` without `-g` is meant for the live command prompt, run while already attached to the one session or window you want to change, not for the config file.

mouse (a session option) is off by default. `set -g mouse on` is the single modern option (tmux 2.1+) that replaces the older, separately-configured mouse-select-pane / mouse-resize-pane / mode-mouse options; once on it enables clicking a pane to focus it, dragging a pane border to resize it, clicking a window's name in the status line to switch to it, dragging inside a pane to select text into copy mode, and wheel-scrolling to enter copy mode automatically.

Once mouse is on, the terminal emulator's own native click-and-drag text selection is superseded by tmux's -- reaching it again needs a modifier key held while dragging (terminal-specific, e.g. Option-drag or Shift-drag), which is expected behavior, not a malfunction.

history-limit (a window option, fixed per-pane at the moment the pane is created) defaults to 2000 lines of scrollback. Raising it, e.g. `set -g history-limit 50000`, only takes effect for panes created after the change -- an already-open pane keeps whatever limit was active when it was born, until it is closed and a new one takes its place.

base-index (a session option) sets the index of the first window created in a session; pane-base-index (a window option) sets the index of the first pane created in a window. Both default to 0. Setting `set -g base-index 1` together with `setw -g pane-base-index 1` renumbers the first window/pane to 1, lining it up with the `1` key used by the default `0`-`9` select-window bindings (chapter 3) instead of leaving the first window sitting on the `0` key at the far end of the number row. The change only applies to windows/panes created after it takes effect, same as history-limit.

renumber-windows (a session option) is off by default: closing a window in the middle of a session leaves a gap in the numbering (0, 1, 3 after closing window 2) rather than shifting the rest down. Turning it on with `set -g renumber-windows on` keeps window numbers contiguous automatically after every close.

escape-time (a server option) defaults to 500 milliseconds -- the time tmux waits after receiving an Escape byte to see whether more bytes immediately follow it (arrow keys and many other special keys begin with the same escape sequence over a terminal connection). That wait is also the noticeable pause felt leaving insert mode in Vim/Neovim inside a tmux pane. Lowering it, e.g. `set -s escape-time 10`, removes the perceptible delay while staying high enough to still recognize genuine escape sequences reliably.

focus-events (a session option) is off by default. Turned on with `set -g focus-events on`, tmux forwards terminal focus-in/focus-out events through to the program running in the active pane; Vim/Neovim use this to support `:set autoread` reloading a file the moment focus returns to that pane after it changed on disk elsewhere (e.g. a git checkout in another pane).

status (session option, on by default) toggles the status line entirely. status-position (session option) defaults to bottom and can be set to top. status-interval (session option) controls, in seconds, how often polled status-line segments (like the clock) refresh, defaulting to 15. Full status-line content and styling (status-left/status-right, colors, segments) is a separate, deeper topic than these baseline toggles.

The community tmux-sensible plugin codifies a commonly-agreed baseline of exactly this kind -- notably a near-zero escape-time and a much higher history-limit than the tmux default -- as a starting point rather than a rulebook; its own README frames itself as settings that should be acceptable to everyone, not a replacement for understanding what each option does.

snippets.code:
# reload the running server's config after an edit
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf

# or, once bound (see the starter config below):
# prefix r
snippets.note: source-file re-reads the file into the already-running server; editing the file alone does nothing until this runs

snippets.code:
# ~/.tmux.conf -- a starter config; see "Configuration Fundamentals" for what each line means
# reload after editing: tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf  (or prefix r, once the binding below is loaded)

# --- server option: one setting for the whole tmux process ---
set -s escape-time 10          # default 500ms -- that's the pause before Esc registers inside Vim

# --- session options: -g sets the default every session inherits ---
set -g mouse on                 # click to focus a pane, drag to resize, drag to select text
set -g history-limit 50000      # default 2000 lines/pane; only affects panes created after this
set -g base-index 1             # windows start at 1, lined up with the 1-9,0 select-window keys
set -g renumber-windows on      # closing a window in the middle closes the gap instead of leaving one
set -g focus-events on          # let Vim/Neovim autoread a file the moment tmux hands it focus back

set -g status-position bottom   # already the default -- written out so it isn't a mystery later
set -g status-interval 5        # default 15s; refresh the status line a little more often

# --- window option: setw -g sets the default every window inherits ---
setw -g pane-base-index 1       # panes start at 1 too, matching base-index above

# worth having before chapter 8 covers key bindings properly:
bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display-message "tmux.conf reloaded"
snippets.note: defaults verified against tmux(1); escape-time/history-limit/mouse/base-index/pane-base-index/status-interval values chosen as reasonable starting points, not tmux's own defaults

pitfalls: Editing ~/.tmux.conf and expecting an already-running session to pick it up automatically -- it only applies to a new server, or once explicitly reloaded with `tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf` (or a bound key that runs the same command).

Writing a bare `set` or `setw` (no -g) at the top of tmux.conf expecting it to become a durable default -- during initial config parsing there may be no current session yet for a non-global session option to apply to, which can outright error; nearly every line in a starting config should use -g, reserving bare set/setw for the live command prompt.

Turning mouse on and being surprised the terminal's own click-drag text selection stops working -- expected: tmux now owns the mouse, and reaching native selection needs a modifier key held while dragging (terminal-specific).
Raising history-limit and finding an already-open pane's scrollback didn't grow -- the new limit only applies to panes created after the change.
Setting base-index/pane-base-index and expecting existing sessions to renumber -- like history-limit, it only affects windows/panes created after the setting takes effect.
